units.name: Basic Economics
units.summary: Why people trade, and what money is for.

topics.name: Why People Trade
topics.summary: How trade leaves both sides better off, and what money solves.

objectives.text: Explain why trade can leave both sides better off.
Describe the problem with barter that money solves.
Explain specialisation and why it increases what is produced.

keyTerms.definition: Exchanging goods or services with someone else.
Trading goods directly for other goods, without money.
Concentrating on producing one thing and trading for the rest.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Trade looks like one person's gain being another's loss. It usually is not, and understanding why explains a great deal about how economies work.

sections.heading: Both sides can gain
sections.body:
A farmer has more rice than she can eat. A fisherman has more fish than he can eat.

They trade some rice for some fish. Now both have rice AND fish.

Nobody lost. Both gained, because each valued what they received more than what they gave up. The farmer had rice going spare; a portion of fish was worth more to her than the tenth bag of rice.

This is the central point: **trade creates value, it does not merely move it.** Nothing new was grown or caught, yet both people are better off than before.

sections.heading: Specialisation
sections.body:
If people can trade, they do not each have to produce everything.

The farmer can spend all her time farming and get good at it. The fisherman can spend all his time fishing. Each produces far more of their one thing than if both split their time between farming and fishing badly.

That is SPECIALISATION, and it is why trade increases the total amount produced, not just who holds it.

It also explains why specialisation depends on trade. Nobody can specialise in fishing alone on an island — they would have fish and nothing else. Specialisation is only safe when you can reliably exchange.
sections.example:
The problem barter cannot solve.

You have rice. You want a shirt. So you find the tailor.

But the tailor does not want rice. He wants shoes.

Now you must find a shoemaker who wants rice, trade rice for shoes, then take the shoes to the tailor. And only if the shoemaker happens to want rice today.

Economists call this the DOUBLE COINCIDENCE OF WANTS: barter needs both people to want what the other has, at the same time.

Money removes the problem entirely. You sell rice to anyone who wants rice, and buy a shirt from the tailor. Neither transaction needs the other person to want what you happen to be holding.

This is what money IS — not wealth in itself, but a thing everyone accepts, so trades no longer have to be matched up in pairs.

sections.heading: What money does
sections.body:
Money does three jobs:

    A MEDIUM OF EXCHANGE — everyone accepts it, so trades need not match.
    A MEASURE OF VALUE — prices let you compare unlike things.
    A STORE OF VALUE — you can sell now and buy later; rice would rot.

The third is why a fisherman can sell a large catch and still eat next month.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Explain how two people can both gain from one trade.
2. Give an example of the double coincidence of wants failing.
3. Why can people specialise only if they can trade?
4. Which job of money matters most to a farmer who harvests once a year? Explain.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Trade can leave both sides better off; it creates value, not just moves it.
• Specialisation raises total production, and depends on being able to trade.
• Barter needs a double coincidence of wants.
• Money is a medium of exchange, measure of value and store of value.

questions.question: How can both people gain from a single trade?
options: One must always lose for the other to gain
Each values what they receive more than what they give up
The trader with more goods always gains
questions.explanation: A farmer with surplus rice values some fish more than her tenth bag of rice, and the fisherman feels the same in reverse. Both end up better off although nothing new was produced. Trade creates value; it does not just move it.

questions.question: What problem with barter does money solve?
options: Barter needs both people to want what the other has, at the same time
Barter cannot be used for food
questions.explanation: This is the double coincidence of wants. With barter you must find someone who has what you want AND wants what you have. Money removes that: you sell to anyone who wants your goods and buy from anyone selling what you need.
